items.title: Measure-preserving transformations and systems
items.statement: A measurable map T:X→X preserves μ when μ(T^-1 E)=μ(E) for every measurable E. A system is (X,A,μ,T). A probability system has μ(X)=1.
items.strategy: Use inverse images throughout; no assumption of invertibility or completeness.

references.title: E–W Definition 2.1, pp.13–14

items.title: Invertible measure-preserving systems
items.statement: An invertible system has a bijective T with measurable inverse. Invertibility modulo null sets means this holds on an invariant conull measurable restriction.
items.strategy: Distinguish actual bijection from invertibility modulo null sets and from measure preservation.

references.title: Einsiedler–Ward Definition 2.1 p.13 and conull restriction convention in Definition 2.7 p.16

items.title: Measure preservation can be checked on a generating pi-system
items.statement: Let T be measurable and P generate A as a pi-system. Suppose P has increasing P_n covering X with μ(P_n)<∞ and μ(T^-1 P)=μ(P) for P in P. Then T preserves μ.
items.strategy: Define ν(E)=μ(T^-1 E); inverse images preserve disjoint unions, so ν is a measure. Apply the exact published uniqueness theorem. For finite measures add X to P.

references.title: E–W §2.1 p.13; local sigma-finite uniqueness theorem

items.title: Compositions, iterates and completions preserve invariance
items.statement: Compositions and nonnegative iterates of measure-preserving self-maps preserve measure. Assuming countable choice for the existence of the completion measure, any measurable measure-preserving self-map of (X,A,μ) remains measurable and measure preserving for the completion (X,Abar,μbar), in particular for a Borel measure and its completion.
items.strategy: Pull back identities; for completion sandwich a completed measurable set between an original measurable set and an original measurable null set, whose preimage is null. The composition and iteration assertions are choice-free; countable choice is used only through the theorem constructing the completion measure, not in the single-set pullback argument.

references.title: Einsiedler–Ward Exercise 2.1.3, p.19; Sarig Proposition 1.4 preservation proof, p.8

items.title: Integral invariance under measure-preserving maps
items.statement: Let T be a measure-preserving transformation. For measurable f≥0, ∫f∘T=∫f in [0,∞]; for integrable real or complex f the same identity holds and f∘T is integrable. Conversely indicator integral invariance implies measure preservation.
items.strategy: Indicators, finite nonnegative simple functions, monotone convergence, then positive/negative and real/imaginary parts.

references.title: E–W Lemma 2.6, pp.15–16

items.title: The Koopman operator
items.statement: For real or complex Lp classes, 1≤p≤∞, define U_T[f]=[f∘T] for a measure-preserving system. The following theorem establishes membership, representative-independence, linearity and isometry.
items.strategy: Pullbacks of null measurable sets are null; therefore the expression is independent of representatives.

references.title: E–W §2.4 pp.28–29; Sarig Proposition 1.3

items.title: Koopman operators are linear isometries
items.statement: For 1≤p≤∞, U_T is a well-defined linear isometry. It is onto for an invertible system.
items.strategy: For finite p use ∫|f∘T|^p=∫|f|^p; at infinity compare all superlevel null sets in both directions. Inverse composition provides surjectivity when applicable. Real quotient facts apply to real functions and moduli only; the complex quotient theorem supplies complex linear operations. For invertibility modulo null sets use the measurable inverse on the invariant conull restriction and zero extension; its inverse preserves restricted measure by applying preservation to T(E). No claim of onto for an arbitrary noninvertible map.

references.title: Einsiedler–Ward §2.4 opening, pp.28–29 (isometry paragraph, not Lemma 2.18)

items.title: Strict and mod-null invariant sigma-algebras
items.strategy: Both families contain only measurable sets. Do not assert they always differ: identity makes them equal.

references.title: E–W Proposition 2.14; Sarig Proposition 1.1

items.title: Both invariant families are sigma-algebras
items.statement: I and I′ are sigma-algebras and I⊆I′.
items.strategy: Complement commutes with pullback; symmetric difference for a countable union is contained in the union of component symmetric differences.

references.title: Sarig Proposition 1.1 proof; E–W Proposition 2.14

items.title: Mod-null invariant sets have strict representatives
items.statement: For E∈I′ the set F=limsup_n T^-n E lies in I and μ(E Δ F)=0.
items.strategy: Each E Δ T^-n E is null by telescoping; the countable union contains E Δ F. Dropping the first term of a limsup proves exact invariance. No completeness needed.

references.title: E–W Proposition 2.14 pp.23–24; Sarig Proposition 1.1 pp.5–6

items.title: Ergodicity relative to an invariant measure
items.statement: T is ergodic for μ if each E∈I has μ(E)=0 or μ(X\E)=0. On a probability space this means measure zero or one.
items.strategy: Name the measure. Permit general measures in the definition, but state subsequent probability hypotheses explicitly.

references.title: Sarig Definition 1.4 p.5

items.title: Equivalent invariant-set and invariant-function criteria for ergodicity
items.statement: On a probability space ergodicity is equivalent to null/conull mod-null invariant sets, to every invariant measurable real or complex function being constant a.e., and to every f with f∘T=f a.e. being constant a.e.
items.strategy: The limsup representative lemma equates strict and mod-null set criteria. For a.e.-invariant real f every rational level set is invariant modulo null sets. Equivalently partition R into dyadic half-open intervals of length 2^-n: exactly one fiber has measure one for each n; their countable intersection is conull and f has a single finite value there. Apply to both components for complex f. Indicators establish all converse directions. Only measurable exceptional sets are removed, so completeness is unnecessary.

references.title: E–W Proposition 2.14 pp.23–25; Sarig Proposition 1.1

items.title: Positive sets sweep out ergodic probability systems
items.statement: In an ergodic probability system, E of positive measure has μ(union_{n≥1}T^-n E)=1. Equivalently every pair A,B of positive measure has μ(B∩T^-n A)>0 for some n≥1.
items.strategy: The union pulls back into itself with equal finite measure, so is mod-null invariant. Use countable subadditivity and the complement of an invariant set for the converses.

references.title: E–W Proposition 2.14 pp.24–25

items.title: Strong and weak mixing on a probability space
items.statement: For a measure-preserving probability system and measurable A,B, Strong mixing means μ(A∩T^-n B)→μ(A)μ(B) for every A,B. Weak mixing means N^-1 sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|μ(A∩T^-n B)-μ(A)μ(B)|→0.
items.strategy: Absolute values occur inside the Cesaro sum. These definitions use probability normalization.

references.title: E–W Definitions 2.32 and 2.35, pp.49–50

items.title: Mixing implies weak mixing, which implies ergodicity
items.statement: Every strongly mixing probability system is weakly mixing; every weakly mixing probability system is ergodic.
items.strategy: Split Cesaro averages into a finite initial segment and small tail; apply weak mixing to a strict invariant set against itself.

references.title: E–W §2.7 pp.49–50; Sarig Proposition 1.2

items.title: Approximation in symmetric difference by a generating algebra
items.statement: If μ(X)<∞ and an algebra C generates A, every E∈A can be approximated in μ(E Δ C) by C∈C.
items.strategy: Let D be the sets approximable in symmetric difference by the generating algebra C. D contains C; complements preserve errors. For E=union E_j with E_j in D and ε>0, continuity from below and μ(X)<∞ give m with μ(E\union_{j≤m}E_j)<ε/2; choose finitely many algebra approximants with total error <ε/2. Thus D is a sigma-algebra and minimality gives D=A. Choices are finite for each tolerance.

references.title: E–W Proposition 2.15 proof and Exercise 2.7.3

items.title: Mixing is checkable on a generating pi-system
items.statement: For a measure-preserving probability system, correlations on a generating pi-system containing X suffice to check strong or weak mixing.
items.strategy: Extend to the algebra of its finite Boolean combinations by finite inclusion-exclusion, then approximate both sets. The error is bounded uniformly in n by twice the sum of their symmetric-difference errors.

references.title: Einsiedler–Ward Exercise 2.7.3(1)–(2), pp.52–53; local Boolean-algebra extension from a pi-system

items.title: Mixing correlations extend to L2 functions
items.statement: For a measure-preserving probability system and complex L2 functions f,g put C_n(f,g)=∫(f∘T^n) conjugate(g) dμ − (∫f dμ)conjugate(∫g dμ). Strong mixing is equivalent to C_n(f,g)→0 for every f,g; weak mixing is equivalent to N^-1∑_{n<N}|C_n(f,g)|→0 for every f,g. The pairing is linear in its first variable.
items.strategy: For indicators this is precisely the set correlation with the two sets interchanged. For finite complex simple sums expand and use the triangle inequality, also inside the Cesaro average. Given ε>0 choose simple a,b with L2 errors <ε using the finite-simple clause of complex density (no smooth-density clause or countable selection). Koopman isometry and complex Cauchy–Schwarz give |C_n(f,g)-C_n(a,b)|≤2(||f-a||2||g||2+||a||2||g-b||2) uniformly in n, since ||1||2=1. This tends to zero with ε. The old real Cauchy–Schwarz edge is used only on the real moduli in the same integral estimate; no equality clause or finite-dimensional projection is used.

references.title: Sarig Proposition 1.3 p.7; E–W Exercise 2.7.7

title: Measure-Preserving Systems and Mixing Criteria — Examples

items.title: A preserving permutation on two equal atoms
items.statement: On X={0,1} with all subsets measurable and μ({0})=μ({1})=1/2, the swap T(0)=1,T(1)=0 preserves μ.
items.strategy: Check the empty, singleton and full sets by inverse images. Countable additivity is finite additivity here because a disjoint family has at most two nonempty members.

references.title: Einsiedler–Ward Definition 2.1, p.13; explicit finite specialization

items.title: A preserving identity need not be ergodic
items.statement: The identity on two atoms of mass 1/2 preserves probability but is not ergodic.
items.strategy: Every inverse image equals the original set; {0} is strictly invariant of measure 1/2, refuting preservation implies ergodicity.

references.title: Sarig Definition 1.4, p.5; explicit finite witness

items.title: The Koopman matrix for a two-point swap
items.statement: For the equal-mass two-point swap, U(a,b)=(b,a), with matrix [[0,1],[1,0]], and ||U(a,b)||p=||(a,b)||p for 1≤p≤∞.
items.strategy: The finite-p norm is ((|a|^p+|b|^p)/2)^(1/p), and the infinity norm is max(|a|,|b|). Both are unchanged by swapping. Establish the underlying preservation directly on the four sets before invoking the theorem.

references.title: Einsiedler–Ward §2.4, pp.28–29; explicit finite specialization

items.title: Finite simple analytic families and their exact endpoint norms
items.statement: Let 1≤p0,p1<∞, 1≤q0,q1≤∞, 0<θ<1, 1/p=(1−θ)/p0+θ/p1, 1/q=(1−θ)/q0+θ/q1, and r=q conjugate, ri=qi conjugate. For finite simple functions f=∑a_j1_Ej and g=∑b_k1_Fk with disjoint finite-measure nonzero fibers, construct coefficientwise entire f_z,g_z, bounded on the closed strip, with f_θ=f,g_θ=g. For nonzero classes ||f_{i t}||p0=||f||p^(p/p0), ||f_{1+i t}||p1=||f||p^(p/p1). If r<∞ then ||g_{i t}||r0=||g||r^(r/r0), ||g_{1+i t}||r1=||g||r^(r/r1), interpreting the exponent as zero at ri=∞ and the norm as one for a nonzero class. If r=∞ (hence q0=q1=1), set g_z=g, retaining ||g_z||∞=||g||∞. Zero classes are treated separately.
items.strategy: For a nonzero coefficient a use phase(a)=a/|a| and exp(p((1−z)/p0+z/p1)log|a|); define zero coefficients identically zero, never log 0 or 0^0. For finite r use the analogous b formula with r((1−z)/r0+z/r1). For r=∞ use constant g. At θ the exponent equals one. On vertical boundaries moduli are fixed powers, yielding the norm identities by finite sums, or the essential maximum for ri=∞. Discard null fibers for nonzero norm claims. Holomorphicity is coefficientwise via the entire exponential and affine composition; no Banach-valued holomorphic theorem is needed.

references.title: Laugesen Appendix C proof of Theorem C.6, pp.170–172, equations (C.4)–(C.6); Teschl Theorem 15.2, p.415

items.title: Riesz–Thorin estimate on the finite simple core
items.statement: On sigma-finite source and target measure spaces, let T be a complex-linear map from complex finite simple a.e. classes of finite-measure support into measurable complex a.e. classes, satisfying ||Tf||qi≤Mi||f||pi for i=0,1, with 1≤p0,p1<∞, 1≤q0,q1≤∞ and finite Mi≥0. Then ||Tf||qθ≤M0^(1−θ)M1^θ||f||pθ for 0<θ<1 and reciprocal-affine exponents. Also the same conclusion holds on arbitrary source and target measure spaces if q0,q1<∞. Endpoint θ=0,1 bounds are the hypotheses, with no 0^0 convention.
items.strategy: Normalize nonzero f and finite simple dual test g to norms one. Use a1, including the constant g family when qθ=1. H(z)=∫(Tf_z)g_z is a finite sum of entire coefficient products times fixed integrals ∫T1_Ej 1_Fk. Those integrals are finite by endpoint Holder and finite-measure test support. This also proves boundedness on the whole closed strip and boundary continuity; no exchanging infinite integrals and derivatives. Endpoint estimates give |H(it)|≤M0 and |H(1+it)|≤M1. Apply exactly thm-hadamard-three-lines, including a zero Mi, then the membership version of the dual-test lemma. Homogeneity recovers arbitrary f; zero f follows from linearity. For arbitrary spaces with finite qi: choose representatives h_j=T1_Ej and set Y0=union_{j,n}{|h_j|>1/n}. Each level set has finite measure since n^(-qi)ν{|h_j|>1/n}≤∫|h_j|^qi. Thus Y0 is sigma-finite and all Tf_z vanish off Y0; run the same dual membership proof on Y0 and extend tests by zero. This proves the full target norm without assuming Tf already belongs to Lqθ or source sigma-finiteness.

references.title: Teschl Theorem 15.2 pp.414–415; Laugesen Theorem C.6 pp.168–173, including p.172 norm-recovery caveat

items.title: Compatible extensions from the finite simple core
items.statement: Assume countable choice and the core hypotheses of the preceding lemma, with its same measure-space alternatives. The finite-simple map extends uniquely as a bounded complex-linear Tθ:Lpθ→Lqθ for every 0≤θ≤1, with the interpolated bounds for 0<θ<1 and original endpoint bounds for θ=0,1. These extensions agree as measurable a.e. classes on every pairwise domain intersection. Consequently the endpoint maps define a well-defined linear map on Lp0+Lp1 by summation, and the interpolated maps are its restrictions.
items.strategy: Density supplies a simple approximating sequence in each finite input exponent; countable choice licenses the selections and representative choices, and complex target completeness (also q=∞) supplies the limit. Norm estimates give independence, uniqueness and linearity. For intersection consistency use a SINGLE simultaneous simple approximation: for fixed f in Lpa∩Lpb truncate to 1/n≤|f|≤n (finite measure because pa<∞), then round both real components toward zero in mesh 1/n² and set the result zero outside the truncation set. Errors tend pointwise to zero and are bounded by 2|f|; dominated convergence of pa and pb powers proves both norm limits (the fixed mesh gives pointwise convergence and rounding toward zero gives the domination). Apply the target a.e.-subsequence theorem successively to this one image sequence in Lqa and Lqb; the two limits coincide off a countable union of measurable null sets, including at infinity. For the sum, two decompositions differ by a member of Lp0∩Lp1, so agreement proves well-definedness. For f in an intermediate Lp, split into |f|>1 and |f|≤1 to get parts in Lp∩Lp0 and Lp∩Lp1 (swap labels if needed); agreement on pairwise intersections proves the restriction claim.

references.title: Teschl Corollary 15.3 p.415 and sum-space discussion p.413; Laugesen Remark C.7(2)–(3) pp.169–170 and proof conclusion pp.172–173

items.title: Interpolate L1 to Linfinity and L2 to L2 bounds
items.statement: On sigma-finite spaces let the same complex-linear finite-simple-core operator satisfy ||Tf||∞≤A||f||1 and ||Tf||2≤B||f||2. For 1<p<2, ||Tf||p-prime≤A^(2/p−1)B^(2−2/p)||f||p. At p=1 and p=2 retain the given endpoint inequalities. The unique bounded extensions are supplied by the preceding corollary under countable choice.
items.strategy: Set θ=2−2/p. Then 1/p=1−θ/2 and 1/p-prime=θ/2. Substitute p0=1,p1=2,q0=∞,q1=2 in a2. For zero constants use a2 at strictly interior θ; state endpoints separately. This is an abstract estimate only: Fourier kernels, Plancherel, Fourier normalization and transform compatibility are future application hypotheses, not premises imported from a later page.

references.title: Laugesen Theorem C.6 pp.168–173; Teschl Corollary 15.4 p.415 as application motivation

items.title: Interpolation for the two-by-two Hadamard matrix
items.statement: On two-point counting measure, H(a,b)=(a+b,a−b) has l1→linfinity norm 1 and l2→l2 norm sqrt(2). Thus for 1≤p≤2 its lp→lp-prime norm is at most 2^(1−1/p).
items.strategy: The infinity estimate follows from |a±b|≤|a|+|b|, sharp at (1,0). Expanding |a+b|²+|a−b|²=2(|a|²+|b|²) proves the second norm exactly. Apply the abstract interpolation bound; countable sums or density are absent in this finite example.

references.title: Laugesen Theorem C.6; explicit finite matrix calculation

items.title: The Hausdorff–Young exponent arithmetic
items.statement: For p=4/3 the parameter is θ=1/2, the target exponent is 4, and the bound from A,B is sqrt(AB). At p=1 the target is infinity, and at p=2 it is 2.
items.strategy: Compute θ=2−2/p and 1/p-prime=1−1/p; the interior coefficient powers are both 1/2. Endpoints refer directly to the two hypotheses.

references.title: Laugesen Remark C.7(1), p.169; explicit specialization

items.title: Finite target bounds do not supply an infinite target bound
items.statement: Assume countable choice, as in the earlier construction of Lebesgue measure. The identity on complex finite simple functions on (0,1) with Lebesgue measure has L1→L1 and L2→L2 bounds one, but has no bounded L1→Linfinity estimate. Thus finite-target interpolation hypotheses alone do not supply an infinite target endpoint.
items.strategy: The finite bounds are identities. For n≥2 take f_n=n 1_(0,1/n); its L1 norm is one and essential supremum n, since its positive set has measure 1/n. Hence a finite L1→Linfinity constant would have to exceed every n. This challenges an invalid inference, not the sound finite-endpoint theorem.

references.title: Laugesen Theorem C.6 and Remark C.7, endpoint parameter scope; explicit witness

items.title: Interpolation of an averaging operator on a probability space
items.statement: On any probability space set Pf=(∫f dμ)1 for finite simple f. It has L1→Linfinity and L2→L2 norms at most one; hence ||Pf||p-prime≤||f||p for 1≤p≤2.
items.strategy: Integral triangle gives the first endpoint. Complex Cauchy–Schwarz against the constant one, whose L2 norm is one, gives the second. Probability spaces are sigma-finite, so apply a4. This operator is defined by a single integral and needs no product-measure or kernel theorem.

references.title: Teschl Theorem 15.2; explicit averaging specialization
